definition: Construct validity is the extent to which a test or assessment appears to measure the underlying ability or process it is intended to measure. In the packet, it is supported by showing that scores on the new device relate in expected ways to established measures of similar motor and cognitive functions.

reasons: The definition misstates construct validity as whether a test “appears” to measure something; that wording fits face validity more than construct validity.

The packet supports construct validity by reporting expected associations with established motor and cognitive measures, but the definition’s first sentence is not supported by the source and is misleading.

The definition’s first sentence (“extent to which a test or assessment appears to measure the underlying ability or process it is intended to measure”) is not explicitly stated in the packet text provided.

The packet supports construct validity only in the narrower, operational sense of demonstrating expected associations between SKILLCOURT outcomes and age-adjusted regression against established motor and seated PC-based cognitive measures; it does not support the broader “extent/underlying ability or process” phrasing.

The proposed support sentence (“scores on the new device relate in expected ways to established measures of similar motor and cognitive functions”) is only partially supported: the packet describes significant age-adjusted regression/prediction against specific established measures (e.g., TUG and PC-based cognitive tasks), but does not explicitly use the wording “similar” or “expected ways” as a general construct-validity criterion.
